item.title: ISAC-Assisted Proactive Handover in mmWave Networks: Value of Foresight and Localization Requirements
item.description: arXiv:2611.03771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) links can lose tens of decibels within milliseconds when a person or vehicle crosses the line of sight, and reactive handover recovers only after the outage has begun. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) promises to let the network see blockers coming and move users to another cell in advance. This paper asks how much such foresight is worth relative to the best reactive handover, and what sensing accuracy is needed to harvest it. We formulate cost-aware cell selection with knowledge of the future signal-to- noise ratio as a sequential decision problem, define the value of foresight through a policy-independent bound, and develop an ISAC-assisted handover framework in which a radio unit senses blockers with its own communication waveform and a simulated Open RAN xApp plans handovers. Ray-traced experiments in a 28 GHz street canyon, reported on held-out scenarios, show that, with a short look-ahead, perfect foresight closes most of the gap between service-aware (Layer-3) reactive handover and an instantaneous oracle. Harvesting this value, however, requires the user and nearby blockers to be localized to about a decimeter, well beyond what our radar tracker and meter- level user positioning provide; with realistic errors, even an uncertainty-aware planner largely defers to reactive handover.
item.dc:creator: Seyed Bagher Hashemi Natanzi, Bo Tang

item.title: Adaptive Low-Rank Quantum Kernel Acquisition under Finite-Shot Measurements: Perturbation Guarantees for QSVMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.03777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum kernel methods require estimating entries of a dense Gram matrix through repeated circuit measurements, making kernel construction expensive and statistically noisy. For a dataset of size $n$, dense construction requires $O(n^2)$ kernel queries, while existing approximation methods typically assume inexpensive access to kernel entries or use non-adaptive sampling. We study adaptive low-rank quantum kernel acquisition when the kernel is accessible only through a finite-shot quantum overlap oracle. Our framework, ICAQKL, uses residual-driven incomplete Cholesky construction to acquire informative kernel columns sequentially and form a positive-semidefinite rank-$r$ surrogate, reducing the training-kernel acquisition cost to $O(nrN_s)$ circuit executions for $r\ll n$, where $N_s$ is the number of shots per queried entry. The central difficulty is that finite-shot errors perturb both the queried kernel values and the adaptive pivot sequence that determines the low-rank factor. We develop a non-asymptotic perturbation framework for this stochastic adaptive process, establishing concentration over the realized queries, stability of noisy pivot selection and factor construction, and propagation of the coupled sampling and approximation errors to the QSVM objective, optimizer, prediction function, and classification margin. The resulting rank--shot conditions characterize when ICAQKL approaches the full QSVM induced by the same quantum feature map. Experiments on benchmark and biomedical datasets show favorable accuracy--query-cost tradeoffs, competitive performance with the full QSVM, and competitive or improved performance relative to the evaluated Nystr\"om baselines under comparable settings. ICAQKL is intended to enable measurement-efficient and theoretically controlled use of a selected quantum kernel, rather than to establish quantum advantage over classical kernels.
item.dc:creator: Duong The Do, Duong Tung Nguyen

item.title: A Modular Open-Source Python Framework for Small Satellite Attitude Determination and Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.03957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advanced attitude determination and control (ADCS) techniques can be difficult for small satellite teams to adopt: tightly coupled implementations require substantial code changes to evaluate different actuators, sensors, orbits, mission goals, and control laws. Existing tools often emphasize orbit mechanics or flight software rather than closed-loop ADCS. This paper presents an open-source, modular ADCS framework in pure Python for rapid development, repeatable testing, and flight-oriented integration across heterogeneous spacecraft. The package supports torque- and command-level control, bound-respecting allocation, and full- and reduced-attitude objectives. Interchangeable estimation, control, planning, and actuator/sensor modules are reconfigured through configuration changes. Integrated simulation includes attitude and orbit propagation, sensor and actuator bias and noise, and environmental disturbances. An actuator-aware planner supports underactuated architectures, while hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) capability enables testing on mission-representative computers. Case studies include a 3U CubeSat with three magnetorquers and one reaction wheel, a magnetorquer-only 1U, and a 6U with three reaction wheels and thrusters. These demonstrate actuator and sensor failures, full- and reduced-attitude goals, and momentum management. HIL testing on a Raspberry Pi uses the same package. Adapting a published control law to a new actuator configuration requires fewer than five lines of configuration changes. The framework underpins flight software for an Earth-observing CubeSat with visible and long-wave infrared imagers, three magnetorquers, and one reaction wheel, without star trackers or propulsion.
item.dc:creator: Patrick McKeen, Niclas Scheuer, Kerri Cahoy

item.title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
item.description: arXiv:2611.03995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.
item.dc:creator: Ali Al Housseini, Jaime Llorca, Cristina Rottondi, Luca Turchet, Tiziano Leidi, Omran Ayoub

item.title: A Review of Max-Pressure Traffic Signal Control Algorithms: State of the Art and Research Opportunities
item.description: arXiv:2611.04029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Max-Pressure (MP) has emerged as a widely studied decentralized traffic signal control framework, thanks to its desirable theoretical properties and strong control performance. Early research on MP focused on improving control performance by exploring different variables of the traffic state for the definition of pressure. Subsequent studies expanded MP to incorporate the complexity of real-world transportation systems and emerging technologies. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these developments. The review first introduces the theoretical foundations of MP and examines early developments in movement weight definition. It then synthesizes major extensions for multimodal and multiscale network control, followed by recent developments in connected and automated vehicle (CAV) environments and the integration of MP with artificial intelligence (AI) and data-driven methods. Beyond summarizing existing approaches, this review examines their underlying assumptions, data requirements, implementation considerations, and practical limitations. Based on this comprehensive review, key research gaps and future directions are identified, including remaining limitations in the theoretical foundations of MP and the underexplored integration of autonomous vehicle control with the MP framework. Overall, this review provides a structured perspective on the evolution and current state of MP control and highlights opportunities for developing more proactive, robust, and practically deployable MP-based traffic control methods.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Al Asif, Chaopeng Tan, Vikash V. Gayah, Hao Liu

item.title: Time to AC-t: When AC-transmission changes capacity expansion planning
item.description: arXiv:2611.04088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capacity expansion models often dramatically simplify the physics of how power flows through a transmission network in order to preserve computational tractability. However, with the rapid growth of electrification, large loads, renewables, and storage, increased realism in planning future grids is imperative. We extend the open-source capacity expansion model GenX with AC optimal power flow physics, and analyze generation, storage, and transmission investment decisions for 20-zone, hourly models of Germany and Texas. We compare our results against those using two common approximations, the transport model and DC optimal power flow. We find that total costs and emissions largely agree across all formulations. However, we find substantial differences in outputs related to transmission, generation siting, storage, and reactive-power support between the approximate formulations and the true AC physics formulation. We identify where AC physics changes planning decisions and discuss how to potentially capture these effects without the full computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Lara Booth, Shiva Madadkhani, Ruaridh Macdonald, Priya L. Donti

item.title: Transferring Controller from Math to Real World Systems: A Formal Control Theoretic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.04163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The letter aims to improve the math-to-real or math-to-sim transfer of a mission controller designed for a Temporal Reach Avoid Stay (T-RAS) specification. Our approach uses the control-theoretic concept of Incremental Input-to-State stability ($\delta$-ISS). We model the real-world system as an uncertain system, represented by a nominal mathematical model with an additive disturbance. Our method involves two steps: firstly, we make the nominal mathematical model and the real-world system $\delta$-ISS. Secondly, we design a mission controller for the mathematical model that satisfies a modified specification. We then prove that applying the same mission-level input sequence to the real-world system guarantees that the original specification is satisfied in the real world. Videos of real-world experiments are available at https://youtu.be/NvjkIZxtnPM.
item.dc:creator: P Sangeerth, Bhabani Shankar Dey, Pushpak Jagtap

item.title: Attack-Aware Intrusion Risk Monitoring for Aerial Surveillance via Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic
item.description: arXiv:2611.04252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers online intrusion-risk assessment and graded warning for unmanned aerial vehicles under bounded measurement attacks. To address this problem, we develop a monitoring framework that combines trusted state estimation, attack-aware risk assessment, and probabilistic signal temporal logic (PrSTL). Trusted observations support recursive state estimation, while potentially attacked observations inform integrity testing and intrusion-risk assessment. The key contribution is a confidence-set construction that combines normalized innovation statistics with physical attack bounds to characterize admissible measurement biases. The resulting family of bias-corrected Gaussian posteriors yields an upper bound on the probability of occupying a no-fly zone or its surrounding safety margin. Confidence guarantees and finite-cover numerical certificates quantify the reliability of this risk envelope, which is evaluated with or without an integrity alarm. The PrSTL monitor analyzes the resulting risk sequence to distinguish ordered, persistent, and repeated risk and produces graded warnings with explicit robustness margins and supporting windows. We validate the monitor in flight experiments with a Crazyflie quadrotor tracked by a Vicon motion capture system. Controlled comparisons quantify the contributions of individual monitoring components. Prescribed risk profiles verify the temporal semantics and illustrate how distinct risk patterns produce different warning levels.
item.dc:creator: Xinhao Yan, Kenji Kashima, Bo Chen, Hailong Huang

item.title: Computing Invariant Reachable Sets through Sum-of-Squares Programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.04325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Funnels, time-varying invariant sets around nominal trajectories, certify that a closed-loop system tracks its plan, and can be composed into verified motion plans. Their computation by sum-of-squares (SOS) programming is well established in formulation but not in practice: the result depends on implementation choices such as the initial guess, Lyapunov function normalization, and termination rule, which the literature documents only briefly. This paper presents a self-contained treatment of SOS-based funnel computation, implemented in the open-source package computeSOSFunnels. We propose a minimum-volume formulation with inlet and outlet constraints under which funnels with coinciding nominal endpoints compose by construction. Numerical experiments on a unicycle, with timing studies on a cart-pole and a 12-state quadrotor, characterize the pipeline: infeasible initial guesses are partly decidable before solving, the certificate shows no violations among 39,000 boundary samples per funnel under the true dynamics, and constructing the semidefinite program, not solving it, dominates computation time.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Khalid M Jaffar

item.title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
item.description: arXiv:2611.04354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.
item.dc:creator: Liang Lin, Jianguo Zhu, Gang Lei, Allen Wang, Xin Lu

item.title: Moving Horizon Estimation and Constrained Model Predictive Control for Balancing a Wheel-Legged Robot Under Unknown Disturbances
item.description: arXiv:2611.04357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wheel-legged robots balance on two wheels while using articulated legs to change height, absorb impacts, and cross uneven terrain. On hardware, the balance controller must rely on noisy inertial and encoder measurements, and it must reject disturbances that are not known in advance, such as payloads and wind, without exceeding motor torque limits. This paper presents a moving horizon estimator (MHE) combined with an offset-free, constrained model predictive controller (MPC) for the sagittal balance of a 9.95 kg wheel-legged robot. The estimator uses a virtual-leg model augmented with a horizontal hip force, a body pitch torque, and a gyroscope bias. Its accelerometer model removes the predicted hip acceleration, and its process noise is increased when an impact is detected. We evaluate the approach in MuJoCo with simulated sensor noise, bias, quantization, and delay, and compare it with LQR baselines that use ground-truth state, a complementary filter, or the same MHE. In a driving, squatting, reversing, and bowing sequence, MPC with MHE reduced the RMS speed error to 0.11 m/s, compared with 0.24 m/s for LQR with ground-truth state. Under an unknown 2 kg payload and a 10 N headwind, the mean position error in wind was 6 cm, compared with 81 cm for LQR with ground-truth state. Across a 3 $\times$ 4 grid of payloads and headwinds, LQR with the same estimator fell in 3 of 12 combinations, compared with 1 of 12 for MPC. These results are limited to simulation on flat ground, and experimental validation on hardware remains future work.
item.dc:creator: Haitham El-Hussieny

item.title: Competition, Switching, and Control in Coupled Adoption-Opinion Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.04407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a Multi-technology AdopTion-opinion co-Evolution (MATE) model to describe the diffusion of $m \geq 2$ competing alternatives within a networked population whose opinions evolve under social influence and the feedback generated by adoption. Communities interact through two layers: a physical network governing exposure to adoption, and a social network shaping opinion evolution through social imitation. Individuals can adopt a technology, eventually becoming dissatisfied at a rate reflecting the quality of the technology, and switch to an alternative at a rate driven by their opinion of that alternative. For an arbitrary number of competing technologies $m \geq 2$, we characterize the equilibria and establish the existence of an adoption-diffused equilibrium in which all technologies coexist. For $m > 2$, the equilibrium configuration depends on the broader competitive environment: unlike the two-technology case, within-community relative adoption generally depends also on equilibrium opinions and on the other alternatives. Finally, we formulate finite-horizon opinion-shaping control problems, derive necessary optimality conditions via the discrete-time Pontryagin maximum principle, and compute numerical extremals using a forward-backward sweep method.
item.dc:creator: Martina Alutto, Fabrizio Dabbene, Angela Fontan, Karl H. Johansson, Chiara Ravazzi

item.title: WiSI: Wireless-in-the-Loop Self-Improvement
item.description: arXiv:2611.04437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents has enabled self-improvement, where agents iteratively refine their programs through execution feedback and performance evaluation. As these agents increasingly operate in physical environments and rely on wireless connectivity, communication conditions become an integral part of their improvement process. However, existing approaches largely assume ideal communication, overlooking how wireless conditions shape both the feedback that guides program modifications and the evaluation outcomes that determine which modifications survive. This challenge is further complicated by the coupling between agent behavior and wireless connectivity, as agents influence their own communication conditions through mobility and transmission decisions. To address this problem, we propose WiSI, a wireless-in-the-loop self-improvement framework that integrates spatiotemporal wireless channels, edge-assisted perception, and Large Language Model-driven program improvement. By incorporating wireless execution into the improvement loop, WiSI reveals how wireless execution experience shapes the generation and retention of program structures, and investigates the wireless conditions needed for robust improvement. Experiments show that agents improved under ideal links achieve only 40.0% task success under congestion, compared with 77.2% when improved under realistic wireless conditions. More importantly, wireless-aware feedback and selection jointly enable agents to discover and retain communication-efficient program structures that outperform parameter tuning and remain robust even with inaccurate run-time channel observations. We further find that moderate-load or mixed-network evaluation maintains strong performance across deployment conditions, while simplified models preserving link-rate statistics achieve comparable results without detailed spatial channel information.
item.dc:creator: Zongxi Liu, Hongyang Du

item.title: Automated consolidation of dispersed DSO data resources into a consistent digital twin of the distribution grid
item.description: arXiv:2611.04463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The energy transition causes a growing number of distributed flexible energy resources in the low voltage grid. To utilize that flexibility, automation and control algorithms are needed, which typically are developed in theoretical research. We build a cyberphysical algorithm test bed to bridge the gap between theoretical research and practical application in cooperation with a local DSO in Walenstadt, Switzerland. To obtain suitable monitoring and data analysis capabilities from their existing data landscape, we propose tool-independent data harmonization measures in preparation for a digital twin of the grid. For data extraction from high-security network zones we developed a secure pipeline that implements a logical data diode ensuring one-way traffic only. Furthermore, we established a test community of voluntary prosumer households, whose flexible assets were made accessible through a common backend, giving us actuation capabilities. The presented publish-subscribe architecture is not only suitable to integrate various data sources into a central data collection, but also to manage access privileges of different stakeholders. This could support unbundling of an organization's data flows and the implementation of data space concepts.
item.dc:creator: Fabian B\"ohm (ETH Z\"urich, Eastern Switzerland University of Applied Sciences), Benjamin Sawicki (ETH Z\"urich), Claudio Stucki (Eastern Switzerland University of Applied Sciences), Pulkit Nahata (ETH Z\"urich), Gabriela Hug (ETH Z\"urich), Lukas Ortmann (Eastern Switzerland University of Applied Sciences)

item.title: Supervised Residual NMPC in Force-Disturbed Quadrotors
item.description: arXiv:2611.04499v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual deployment can affect closed-loop tracking. We compare two ways to deploy one supervised acceleration-residual network in nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) of a quadrotor. Cyclewise deployment repeats one correction across the horizon. Stagewise deployment evaluates shifted prediction nodes before the solve. Network parameters remain fixed during control. On prescribed force pulses, both schemes improve average tracking mainly after force removal, but worsen hover; some prediction checks also fail. Seed 1 reinforcement-learning benchmarks add no mean benefit under pulses or prescribed random forces. On 220 conditions, cyclewise and stagewise supervision reduce mean integral absolute position error (IAE) by 4.38% and 7.77%. On a separate 32-condition bank, fixed gain 1.5 lowers IAE by 27.47% relative to stagewise supervision but raises angular-rate root-mean-square error by 10.19%. In one synthetic computational fluid dynamics field, stagewise supervision lowers four-task mean IAE by 2.01% against a same-graph zero-residual control; some secondary metrics worsen. These simulations show that residual deployment affects tracking, with gains and limitations that depend on task and motion metric.
item.dc:creator: Shenghan Sun

item.title: On the IQC and SRG Frameworks: Equivalences and Converse Results
item.description: arXiv:2611.04593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) and scaled relative graphs (SRGs) are two prominent frameworks for analyzing feedback systems. Although both frameworks are rooted in the same graph separation principle, a general characterization of their relationship has remained unavailable. This paper establishes conditions under which the IQC- and SRG frameworks are equivalent. To this end, we introduce two new classes of systems, termed disjunctive and conjunctive systems, which are respectively characterized by unions and intersections of quadratic input-output constraints. Under structural assumptions, we prove equivalence between the IQC and SRG frameworks for these system classes. By exploiting this equivalence, we develop novel IQC- and SRG-based converse stability results for linear and nonlinear systems. Our results accommodate multiple quadratic constraints, extending well-known converse results in robust control beyond the single-constraint setting.
item.dc:creator: Sebastiaan van den Eijnden, Chao Chen, Sei Zhen Khong

item.title: TuneBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Power System Dynamic Model Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.04640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can automate complex engineering workflows by interacting with tools, interpreting feedback, and making iterative decisions. This paper introduces TuneBench, a benchmark for evaluating Agentic AI in power system dynamic model calibration, where controller parameters are adjusted to reproduce target dynamic responses. The benchmark reflects a common Transmission System Operator (TSO) practice, in which equivalent models used for Dynamic Security Assessment (DSA) are calibrated against measurements from grid-code compliance tests when proprietary models are unavailable. Two cases of increasing complexity are considered: the governor and Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) of a synchronous generator and the control system of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), both tuned against active-power and voltage step tests within a budget of 15 simulations. LLM-based agents are compared with random search and Genetic Algorithm (GA) baselines over 10 independent runs. Only the most advanced models, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6, accurately reproduce all target trajectories, with median R2 above 0.995 in every test and tracking errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than the baselines. The agent logs show that these agents autonomously extract dynamic performance indices, such as settling time and damping, and relate them to specific control parameters, decomposing the tuning problem into physically interpretable sub-problems. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/Power-Agent/PowerAgentBench/tree/main/benchmarks/dynamic/level3.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Pomarico, Salvatore Tessitore, Giorgio Giannuzzi, Alberto Berizzi

item.title: Multi-experiment identification from short repeated transients:the human response to pushes in a Tai Chi posture
item.description: arXiv:2611.04761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The effect of Tai Chi postures on the mechanical response of the body to external pushes is usually assessed with clinical balance scores, which say little about the underlying dynamics. We identify, for five subjects and eight postural conditions, linear models from the mechanical work transferred by a pendulum hitting the forearm to the change of the antero-posterior ground reaction force. Each trial contains 10 to 16 impacts, and each impact yields a transient of 0.55\,s only. Building on earlier analyses of these data, we improve the processing chain in three ways. The input is related to the energy lost by the pendulum and its repeatability is quantified. The output is defined component-wise, which makes it independent of the zeroing of the force plate. Finally, the impacts are stacked in a multi-experiment least-squares problem and validated on unseen impacts. Tenth-order ARX models then reach a median leave-one-impact-out fit of 65\%, against 72\% for the repeatability of the response itself, and never require stability enforcement, unlike estimation on averaged impacts. Closing the eyes lengthens the identified delay by about 70\,ms in all subjects, and the Tai Chi posture increases the antero-posterior force transmitted per joule in four of five subjects. Surface EMG envelopes show a tonic co-activation of the lower-leg muscles in this posture, a smaller reactive triceps burst and a fast habituation of the tibialis response. Together, they point to a stiffer, anticipatory postural strategy.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel Witrant (GIPSA-INFINITY), Olivier A. J. Martin (GIPSA-DSD), Pascal Bellemain (GIPSA-Services)

item.title: TriMedium: A Cross-Medium Simulator for Embodied Networking Across Air-Ground-Sea
item.description: arXiv:2611.04763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied intelligent applications have expanded from air and ground into maritime environments, where missions such as coastal reporting require coordination among underwater sensing, surface gateways, and aerial relays. Yet field trials remain costly, and existing simulation tools make it difficult to study how cross-medium communication affects cooperation among these platforms. We present TriMedium, an integrated Air-Ground-Sea simulator for cross-medium embodied networking. TriMedium has three design elements. First, it provides a shared three-dimensional world where aerial, terrestrial, and underwater entities coexist, so underwater agent motion and visual observations stay geometrically consistent with air and ground nodes. Second, it uses a common simulation clock that preserves observation timestamps while scheduling delayed communication and computation, clarifying when the shore receiver obtains each observation. Third, modular quantization and compression interfaces accommodate heterogeneous telemetry and image pipelines, while integrity checks separate intentional lossy distortion from incomplete or corrupted delivery. Three case studies validate TriMedium. Multimodal data delivery tests telemetry and image pipelines, scene construction examines cross-domain spatial consistency, and positioning assesses geometric accuracy under delayed communication. Together, they show TriMedium enables embodied networking by quantifying cross-medium delivery dynamics and fidelity across heterogeneous payloads.
item.dc:creator: Ruizhe Dang, Jiayi Su, Wenlihan Lu, Weijie Yuan, Shijian Gao

item.title: Assignment-Free Swarm Navigation via Adaptive Target-Field Planning and Mean-Shift Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.04824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mean-shift exploration enables assignment-free swarm shape assembly, but obstacle-constrained navigation additionally requires coordinated adaptation of the desired morphology and its physical execution. This paper presents an environment-adaptive navigation framework that integrates target-field planning, execution regulation, and morphology-preserving mean-shift exploration. A feasibility-aware graph search plans the position, orientation, and morphology of an unlabeled target field without specifying robot-specific goals. An execution-regulated reference manager adjusts field progression and morphology switching using swarm entering, coverage, and lag metrics. A moving-frame controller separates prescribed rigid motion from local mean-shift redistribution and incorporates neighbor interactions and obstacle responses. Simulations and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework coordinates morphology transitions and collective motion for assignment-free swarm navigation through cluttered environments.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxuan Li, Junhui Zhang, Bo Zhu

item.title: Sufficient and Necessary Smooth Barrier-Like Conditions for Continuous-Time Finite-Horizon Safety Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.04888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-horizon safety verification for continuous-time stochastic systems modeled by stochastic differential equations. Given an open and bounded safe set, a compact initial set, a finite time horizon, and a prescribed violation-probability threshold, the objective is to certify that the exit probability from the safe set before the horizon remains below the threshold. Under uniform ellipticity of the diffusion matrix and regularity of the safe-set boundary, we develop a time-dependent barrier-like condition expressed as a set of functional inequalities, obtained by relaxing a parabolic initial-boundary value problem associated with the exit probability. If a function satisfies the condition, then the probability of leaving the safe set before the horizon is guaranteed to remain below the threshold. Conversely, when the exit probability is strictly smaller than the prescribed threshold uniformly over the initial set, the barrier-like condition is also necessary: there exists a smooth function satisfying it. Furthermore, when the dynamics are polynomial and the set descriptions are semialgebraic, the problem of verifying the condition admits a sum-of-squares formulation that is both sound and complete, yielding a complete degree hierarchy for finite-horizon stochastic safety verification.
item.dc:creator: Bai Xue

item.title: On the Convexity of Common Resource Adequacy and Capacity Accreditation Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2611.04896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many emerging capacity expansion optimization formulations implicitly presume the convexity (or concavity) of power system adequacy risk (or capacity accreditation) metrics. These assumptions have yet to be formally justified. We present concise mathematical proofs validating the claim for certain metrics (expected unserved energy and effective load carrying capability), but also provide simple invalidating counterexamples for others (loss-of-load expectation and equivalent firm capacity). Formulations built on non-convex (non-concave) metrics structurally undervalue candidate portfolio adequacy, and so cannot claim to produce least-cost expansion plans.
item.dc:creator: Gord Stephen

item.title: A Matrix-Separation Approach for Stability of Discrete-Time Systems with Time-Varying Delay
item.description: arXiv:2611.04928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter addresses the stability analysis of discrete-time linear systems with time-varying delay using a Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional (LKF) framework. An improved matrix-separation-based inequality (IMSBI) is developed to obtain tighter bounds for the summation terms arising in the forward difference of the LKF. Based on this result, an augmented LKF incorporating additional cross-terms is constructed to capture the interaction between system states and delay evolution. This leads to a less conservative delay-dependent stability criterion expressed as linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). Numerical results demonstrate improved stability margins and a reduced number of decision variables compared with existing methods.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: N. Echakroune, E. Houssaine Tissir and S. Belamfedel Alaoui, "A Matrix-Separation Approach for Stability of Discrete-Time Systems With Time-Varying Delay," in IEEE Control Systems Letters, vol. 10, pp. 2125-2130, 2026
item.dc:creator: Nabil Echakroune, El Houssaine Tissir, Sadek Belamfedel Alaoui

item.title: From Roadside Sensing to Risk-Informed Safety Control: Surrogate Safety Measures as a Cyber-Physical Interface
item.description: arXiv:2611.04988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proactive intersection safety analysis depends on trajectory data whose reliability varies by sensing modality, yet infrastructure-perception and surrogate safety measure (SSM) research have only recently begun to converge. This paper synthesizes both literatures alongside control theory to clarify how sensing choices, safety metrics, and predictive control connect end-to-end, and where infrastructure-derived risk signals could inform autonomous vehicle decision-making. Searches covered light detection and ranging (LiDAR), cooperative perception, time-to-collision (TTC), post-encroachment time (PET), extreme value theory, model predictive control (MPC), and signal control. Screening considered trajectory-based safety and control relevance, excluding detection benchmarks without safety linkage. This structured narrative synthesis retained 56 sources. No single SSM is universally valid: one-dimensional TTC and modified TTC suit longitudinal conflicts, two-dimensional TTC extends time-based measurement to crossing geometries, and observed PET captures crossing and vulnerable road user (VRU) conflicts but only after the event. LiDAR consistently outperforms camera-only sensing for continuous three-dimensional trajectory extraction, illumination robustness, and privacy, though its range degrades in heavy rain, fog, and snow. Its output becomes control-ready only when paired with filtering--Kalman, Savitzky-Golay--that stabilizes noisy detections. This review complements it from the infrastructure side: it examines how roadside sensing affects that chain's reliability, classifies SSMs by conflict geometry and temporal availability, and maps risk components onto control objectives and constraints for infrastructure and connected and automated vehicle (CAV) applications.
item.dc:creator: Salsabil Salah, Yiqiao Li, Bo Wang

item.title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
item.description: arXiv:2611.05031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.
item.dc:creator: S{\o}lve Eidnes, H{\aa}kon Noren Myhr

item.title: Graph-Based Dynamic Activity Prediction for Real-Time Power System Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.05077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online dynamic security assessment and day-ahead planning require rapid identification of where disturbances will produce significant dynamic activity. Full time-domain simulations are computationally demanding, while existing machine-learning approaches predict system-level outcomes or require post-disturbance trajectories. This paper proposes a pair-aware Graph Isomorphism Network with Edge features (GINE) framework comprising two task-specific models for predicting bus-voltage and generator apparent-power activity from the operating point and contingency description. Physically aware KPI cuts convert simulated responses into ordinal activity targets for model training. Evaluations on Nordic 32 and the French transmission system with more than 6 000 buses show that pair-aware fusion and graph embeddings improve on a local baseline on Nordic 32, with GINE the lower-cost graph encoder, and that the framework remains effective at large scale. As a downstream application, the predicted activity maps guide Adaptive Model Simplification, reducing continuous and discrete model variables by 72% and 66%, achieving speedups of up to 3.16x, and preserving voltage trajectories when critical substations are retained. These results demonstrate scalable, pre-disturbance prediction of component-level dynamic activity.
item.dc:creator: Stefanos Eleftheriadis, Mohammad Hashemnezhad, Savvas Panagi, Thibaut Vermeulen, Petros Aristidou

item.title: Stray Losses in Power Transformers: A Comparative Study of Modeling Frameworks for Mild Steel
item.description: arXiv:2611.05109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately predicting eddy-current and hysteresis losses in mild steel components such as the structural parts and tank of power transformers remains a challenge in transformer design. Conventional numerical approaches for eddy-current loss analysis require discretization at a fraction of the skin depth. While accurate, such fine volumetric mesh becomes computationally prohibitive for large power transformers. Moreover, hysteresis loss is not always included in this analysis. To investigate the trade-off between computational cost and accuracy, this work presents a comparative analysis of eight distinct modeling frameworks for predicting both eddy-current and hysteresis losses in mild steel. These include efficient methods avoiding meshing, such as standard impedance boundary conditions, and more accurate approaches retaining full volumetric meshing, namely complex permeability, nonlinear single-valued B-H curve, and Jiles-Atherton hysteresis modeling. To accurately represent the material's electromagnetic behavior, the properties of the mild steel used are measured directly from samples. Finally, loss measurements are conducted to benchmark all eight frameworks, demonstrating mean absolute percentage errors between predictions and measurements generally below 20%.

item.title: The Novelty Horizon H_N: Why Large Language Models Fail to Generate Scientific Data beyond Their Training Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.05175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) lack physical grounding and extrapolation. This paper formalises the Novelty Horizon as tasks needing extrapolation beyond training support, causal reasoning absent from learned correlations, or post-frontier information. A forensic analysis tests LLMs on unguided, guided, and ground-truth data from an underrepresented diode-clamped short-circuit experiment using temporal, spectral, and statistical validation against a first-principles Modified Ohm's Law. Both script-based approaches fail catastrophically with physical and spectral inconsistencies, extreme statistical pathologies, zero Generative Fidelity Score, and linear-regime outputs. Direct prompting corroborates distinct failure modes. This paper introduces the Past Information Boundary and physics-based authentication. LLM data generation cannot extrapolate past the Novelty Horizon essential for novel discovery. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems must preserve human causal reasoning and experimental design.
item.dc:creator: Alex Mwololo Kimuya, Mary Mwadulo, Dickson Mwenda Kinyua

item.title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.
item.dc:creator: Javal Vyas, Mehmet Mercang{\"o}z

item.title: Learning curves in natural and artificial systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.05224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A general mathematical model of experience formation is considered, in which the learning level is defined as the probability that the next value of the uncertainty factor has already been mastered and not forgotten. Within this model the shape of the learning curve is derived, and it turns out to be determined primarily by the distribution of situation occurrence: a uniform distribution yields an exponential curve, whereas a power-law distribution yields a power-law curve whose exponent equals the ratio of the distribution exponent to that same exponent increased by one. Both mechanisms generating power-law curves, established earlier in the analysis of debugging, assembly and repair activities, are shown to have been independently rediscovered in deep learning theory as the "frequency" and "spectral" mechanisms of scaling laws for artificial neural networks, while the exponential curves of machine learning (contraction operators, strongly convex optimization, stationary reinforcement) are generated by the same constancy of the contraction coefficient that was revealed half a century earlier in models of radioactive decay, the first-order lag element, and others. A solution is given for the problem of choosing a training distribution that differs from the deployment distribution. A methodological consequence is discussed: three distinct mechanisms generate curves indistinguishable in shape, so an observed learning curve does not allow one to judge the "internal" structure of the learning system.
